title: Apple Seeks 200,000 People for AI Health Study

content_html:
Monday November 16, 2026 3:13 am PST by Tim Hardwick

Apple on Sunday announced the launch of an Apple Health AI Usage Study that gives participants access to a dedicated iPhone app that answers everyday health questions using medical research and, optionally, their own Health app data.


Conducted in collaboration with clinical AI company OpenEvidence, the U.S.-only study will examine how people understand and evaluate AI-generated health information, what makes them trust it, and whether it can help them prepare for appointments with their doctors.

"At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life," said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness. "Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey."

The app combines OpenEvidence's technology with an Apple-designed research experience, where responses include links to peer-reviewed clinical sources, with information drawn from publications like The New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA, and Nature. Apple says the app presents complex medical information in approachable language.


Participants can choose to share data such as their resting heart rate, activity, sleep, and lab results through HealthKit. The idea is for it to allow researchers to explore whether incorporating personal health information makes answers more relevant and easier to understand. Apple says the app can also help users put Health data in context, understand symptoms or conditions, and build personalized exercise or meal plans.

Users can rate responses and complete occasional surveys about their experience, and all questions undergo processing designed to remove identifying information before reaching OpenEvidence, which deletes question-and-response data within 24 hours. Apple says study data will not be used to train AI models, and participants control whether they share HealthKit metrics or survey responses.

"Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds," said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF's professor and chair of the Department of Medicine. "When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Connecting these tools, and rigorously studying what works, is how we'll get there."

Apple is keen to stress that health tools powered by large language models can give incomplete or unclear answers, and the app includes safeguards that are meant to detect certain concerning questions and direct users toward a healthcare provider or other resources. The study isn't intended to diagnose or treat conditions, or replace advice from medical professionals.


The study is open to up to 200,000 eligible U.S. residents aged 21 and older with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone running iOS 26 or later. If you're eligible and interested, download the Apple Health AI Study App from the App Store to learn more.
